title: Object There Was None
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from "The Tell-Tale Heart" by Edgar Allan Poe (1843), collected in The Works of Edgar Allan Poe.
body: It is impossible to say how first the idea entered my brain; but once conceived, it haunted me day and night. Object there was none. Passion there was none. I loved the old man. He had never wronged me. He had never given me insult. For his gold I had no desire. I think it was his eye! yes, it was this! He had the eye of a vulture—a pale blue eye, with a film over it. Whenever it fell upon me, my blood ran cold; and so by degrees—very gradually—I made up my mind to take the life of the old man, and thus rid myself of the eye forever.

Now this is the point. You fancy me mad. Madmen know nothing. But you should have seen me. You should have seen how wisely I proceeded—with what caution—with what foresight—with what dissimulation I went to work! I was never kinder to the old man than during the whole week before I killed him. And every night, about midnight, I turned the latch of his door and opened it—oh, so gently! And then, when I had made an opening sufficient for my head, I put in a dark lantern, all closed, closed, that no light shone out, and then I thrust in my head.

Upon the eighth night I was more than usually cautious in opening the door. A watch’s minute hand moves more quickly than did mine. Never before that night had I felt the extent of my own powers—of my sagacity. I could scarcely contain my feelings of triumph. To think that there I was, opening the door, little by little, and he not even to dream of my secret deeds or thoughts.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did the narrator claim he had no desire for?
options: The old man's gold
The old man's house
The old man's respect
The old man's forgiveness

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what did the narrator say it was about the old man that bothered him?
options: His eye
His voice
His laugh
His hands

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did the old man's eye look like?
options: A pale blue eye, with a film over it
A bright green eye that glowed
A dark brown eye, bloodshot and wide
A milky white, sightless eye

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what did the narrator carry into the old man's room each night?
options: A dark lantern, all closed
A lit candle
A sharpened knife
A pocket watch

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the narrator insist he loved the old man and had no motive against him?
options: To argue his actions weren't driven by ordinary reasons like hatred or greed, making his fixation on the eye seem stranger
To convince the reader that he never actually harmed the old man
To explain why he later confessed to the crime
To show that the old man had forgiven him in advance

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why was the narrator especially kind to the old man during the week before the murder?
options: His kindness was part of his careful, deceptive plan
He was having second thoughts about his plan
The old man had recently done him a favor
He wanted witnesses to remember him fondly

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the narrator compare his own patience to a watch's minute hand?
options: To emphasize just how slowly and carefully he moved the door open
To show that he was constantly checking the time
To suggest that time seemed to stand still with fear
To explain why he was late arriving that night

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the narrator feel triumphant on the eighth night?
options: He believed his secret plan was working perfectly without the old man suspecting anything
He had finally decided to abandon his plan
The old man had invited him into the room
He had found a way to return the gold he'd stolen

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the overall point of the passage?
options: The narrator methodically and patiently plotted to kill the old man because of an obsessive fixation on his eye
The narrator accidentally caused the old man's death during an argument
The narrator and the old man were plotting together against a third person
The narrator was trying to protect the old man from an unknown threat

questions.prompt: As used in the passage, what does it mean that the narrator acted with "dissimulation"?
options: Concealment of one's true feelings or intentions
Extreme physical caution
Open honesty about one's plans
A sudden burst of anger

questions.prompt: According to the passage, when did the idea of killing the old man begin to haunt the narrator?
options: Once it was conceived, it haunted him day and night
Only on the night he acted
Years after he first met the old man
After the old man insulted him

questions.prompt: Per the passage, at what time did the narrator open the old man's door each night?
options: About midnight
At dawn
Just after dinner
In the middle of the afternoon

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how did the narrator describe the way he opened the door?
options: So gently
Loudly and carelessly
With a sudden shove
Only partway

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what had the narrator never felt before the eighth night?
options: The extent of his own powers, of his sagacity
Any fear of being caught
Sympathy for the old man
Doubt about his plan

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why might the narrator's insistence that "object there was none, passion there was none" actually suggest something troubling about his state of mind?
options: It suggests an unmotivated obsession rather than a rational reason for wanting to kill
It proves that he was acting in self-defense
It shows he was being blackmailed by the old man
It confirms that the old man provoked him repeatedly

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes the narrator's account of the eighth night?
options: He was more careful than ever, savoring how close he came to catching the old man completely unaware
He gave up his plan out of guilt
He was caught by the old man before he could act
He decided to confess everything to the old man

questions.prompt: As used in the passage, what does it mean that the narrator felt his own "sagacity"?
options: Wisdom or shrewdness in judgment
Physical strength
Deep sadness
Uncontrollable fear
